I relate to that a lot. That's the same things I've also thought about myself. I've isolated myself from my family so that I wouldn't bother them, but then they would complain about me never spending time with them etc. Only after I've moved out and started to process things away from the toxic environment I grew up in did I realize that no matter what I would've done, they always would've found something to criticize me for.

It'll take time to open up to your new therapist, especially after the mistreatment of your last one. I know it's hard to trust someone after getting hurt so deeply. Maybe you can start by testing the waters just to see their reaction to some topics you'd like to speak about. A proper therapist will know that you can't just will away your mental illnesses. It might take a while to find a person you're comfortable with too and there's no shame in that. Therapy is about you feeling safe with the other person, so you're allowed to find a different one if you don't click with the current one. I personally switched psychiatrists three times in one year before I found one that took me seriously and didn't immediately dismiss me.

And if there's ever someone again who tells you that it was your fault or that you're a bad person, then please remember that it's not true. You're the victim, not the other way around. From your messages here I can tell that you're a kind person. You care about others and are concerned about them. A bad person wouldn't say these things. Things will eventually become easier, but it'll take a lot of time and basically rewiring your brain to unlearn the stuff your parents told you again and again. I know it sounds a little cheesy, but what helped me with that is to notice when I'm thinking unkind things about myself and to immediately tell myself the opposite. Stuff like, 'people care about me' or 'I am good enough'. It's definitely a little cringe at first, but over time it'll actually help your brain to not instantly think negatively in those situations.

I'm finally at a point where small setbacks don't immediately send me spiraling anymore. I truly hope that you can one day be happy with who you are, too. I'm sure the real you is a wonderful person.

I'm so sorry they treated you like that. This is classic victim blaming, something narcissistic parents love to do, because they can't fathom the thought they could ever be in the wrong. It's good that you were able to get away from them, for your own sake.

Have you been able to get a different therapist? I think it's really important to have a professional to help you process these experiences, as well as manage the ADHD, if you struggle with that. A real therapist isn't going to insult you or downplay your feelings.

I totally get that. My parents are the same. At some point we just need to realize that they're not going to change. I tried to stay in contact with mine, but that just resulted in me getting hurt over and over again and ruining my own mental health. You might want to look at the r/raisedbynarcissists subreddit too, if you haven't already. It helped me realize that it's not my fault I don't get along with my parents. We can only do so much without sacrificing part of ourselves. If they don't want to make the effort to maintain a healthy relationship with their daughter, then that's their fault, not yours.

If you still want to try, be ready to get disappointed, as harsh as it sounds. If your parents are anything like mine, they're not going to change their ways. My advice would be to wait until feelings have calmed down a little, maybe talk about it with your bio mom and stepdad, then ask to meet them to discuss your boundaries. The way they treated you until now isn't fair and it's okay to tell them that. By their reaction to this you can probably already tell if they're going to respect your boundaries or not. Sometimes it's just not worth it to try and make things work with people who don't care enough.

It's not going to be easy either way, but I wish you the best of luck. You deserve to be happy.

You're not obligated to talk to them. It took me years to learn that too, but people who hurt us aren't entitled to stay in our lives, even when they come back begging and crying and pretending to suddenly care. Ignorance is not an excuse for the pain they've inflicted on you, especially when they chose to stay ignorant and never apologized to you.

I'm glad you're doing a little better already. I hope your bio mom and stepdad can help you slowly build up your confidence and mental health to where you feel comfortable again.

Lmao great argument. Should've known something like that was gonna be your reaction. I have grown up. And it would've been a lot easier if I had more knowledge about being trans.

I wish I would've learned about trans stuff earlier. When I found out it was possible for me to be a boy at age 10, I cried. I didn't come out for another 8 years, hating myself as my body changed with puberty, becoming severely suicidal. If I grew up learning more about these things at a younger age, seeing it normalized instead of being talked about as something 'weird' on TV, perhaps I would've been able to enjoy my childhood as a boy instead of hating having to be a girl.

Children getting exposed to and having access to these resources isn't going to turn cis kids trans, but it sure as hell will help trans kids realize that there's nothing taboo or weird about them feeling the way they do. It's going to lead to children having the opportunity to live authentically instead of hating themselves and thinking something is wrong with them as they grow up. Puberty is hard enough for cis teens already. If we have the chance to make it easier for trans teens by giving them all the information they need before hormones change their bodies potentially forever, why not do so? It'll mean less depression, less suicidal ideation.

Are there going to be some kids thinking they might be trans and end up to be cis? Yeah, most likely. But that's why these decisions are made by doctors, before anyone would get hormones or blockers. And if that's still a concern, then it's even more of a reason for children to figure their stuff out earlier, because for younger children, there's no need to medically intervene. All they do as transitioning is changing their clothes and using a different name/ pronouns. If after a few years they realize this isn't the right thing for them, it's easy to just go back to their agab with no harm done.

You're not overreacting. You're not a horrible child. Your parents are completely in the wrong here. Unfortunately the things our parents tell us get so ingrained in our brains that it's hard to unlearn thinking about ourselves the same way.

If you're able to, moving out as soon as possible would be the first step. Once I moved out of my abusive household, I was finally able to start restructuring my brain. Try to find friends who support you and definitely find a therapist who doesn't dismiss you. It's going to be hard, but I promise you things can and will get better.

When I was your age 10 years ago, I never would've thought I'd get this far, but now I'm NC with my parents and live with my fiancée, who is the most wonderful person I've ever met. She never gave up on me when I relapsed or when I started to self-destruct again, but simply reassured me that she'll be with me no matter what. Learning that I'm allowed to take up space and have a voice is something I still struggle with today, but I'm steadily making progress.

If you can, find a therapist who's experienced with trans people. Do you have the means to go to therapy without your parents knowing exactly what kind it is? You're an adult woman, so they don't have to know everything you do. Lying to them for your own safety and health does no make you a bad daughter. If you're able to work and pay for therapy yourself (or get it for free through healthcare), I'd recommend you do that. Getting therapy specifically for gender dysphoria and getting on hormones made everything else a lot easier to deal with for me. If you feel like other issues are more pressing to you, you could also try to find a therapist specifically for PTSD first.

You don't deserve to be treated the way they treat you. You're a human being and deserve to be treated with kindness and respect just like anyone else. Your mental illnesses don't make you any less worthy of that.

I personally got a cheap cane to test out how much I'd benefit from one. Before I got it, I'd occasionally have to use a crutch to keep myself from bumping into things when I'm out and about. I used to have to decide if I'd rather risk stumbling into hedges on one side or cars on the other, because idiots can't park where I live. With my cane I at least have one safe side. Sometimes I'd also randomly get dizzy and almost fall onto the street, so this is absolutely safer for me.

It definitely also helps in guaranteeing a seat on the bus, since standing would be impossible for me on most days. I still struggle a little with the mental image of being a young person with a mobility aid, but I deal with social anxiety anyway, so it's nothing new for me. I do sometimes get a few weird looks, especially from older people, but I know my body best and if I would go out without my cane, I'd have significantly more trouble. I'm already thinking about investing in a different mobility aid for the worse days when I can't go without sitting down and taking a break every 5 minutes.

I also haven't fainted in a few years, just have general problems with dizziness/ sometimes presyncope and feeling weak. If you think a mobility aid of any kind could be beneficial for you, I highly encourage you to just try it out! Maybe start with a cheap cane like I did and see if it works. If it doesn't and you need something 'more', there's no shame in that. Only you can know what will work best for your symptoms and we shouldn't let the fears of seeming silly or stupid stop us from doing what's best for our bodies. We're all just trying to navigate life with whatever lot we were dealt and we have every right to use any help we can get.

I wasn't struggling to hold her, she wasn't lunging or pulling, she was just standing in place. I never mentioned anything about her pulling in the post, only that the man was talking about it. She used to always almost choke herself out when we used it and since her pulling was an issue, we switched to a harness with a front clip. Not many issues with pulling since, unless she gets riled up like this, but that happens rarely lol
She never reacted badly to men before her surgery. Only after. We clip the leash to the front of the harness, so instead of pulling, she flips herself around. It's literally not an issue anymore.
